note_claims.claim: The patient presented with increased exertional breathlessness and palpitations for three weeks, on a background of atrial fibrillation diagnosed 18 months ago.
The patient reports symptoms including breathlessness on stairs, palpitations, occasional postural light-headedness, and mild evening ankle swelling.
The patient is prescribed Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, Bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily, and Levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily.
Examination findings include an irregularly irregular pulse at 104 bpm, blood pressure of 128/76, fine bibasal crackles, and mild bilateral ankle oedema.
ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of approximately 105.
The patient has reduced renal function (creatinine 140) and atrial fibrillation with suboptimal rate control, likely contributing to breathlessness.
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is appropriate due to weight (58 kg) and creatinine (140).
A single episode of rectal bleeding on anticoagulation requires investigation.
The plan is to increase the bisoprolol dose to 5 mg once daily and arrange an echocardiogram within six weeks.
The apixaban dose will be continued at 5 mg twice daily.
Investigations planned include a Full Blood Count (FBC), a FIT test, and consideration for a lower GI referral.

Safety netting advises attending A&E for further significant bleeding, black stools, or feeling faint, and calling 999 if breathing worsens significantly, especially lying flat, or if chest pain occurs.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician is Dr. Sandhu, a cardiology registrar.
Patient's daughter is Rosalind.
Patient was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation about eighteen months ago.
Patient reports feeling more puffed out lately, going up the stairs, and feeling heart fluttering.
Symptoms (breathlessness/palpitations) have been present for three weeks, perhaps a little more.
Patient denies chest pain.
Patient experiences light-headedness once or twice when standing up quickly, but has not fainted.
Patient reports ankles swelling, a little, by the evening.
Patient can lie flat at night on one pillow, same as always.
Clinician asks how the patient is taking apixaban.
Patient initially states taking apixaban once a day in the morning.
Relative corrects the frequency: it is taken twice a day (morning and night), and the relative fills the dosette box every Sunday.
Patient confirms the correction: 'Oh, is it? Yes, she does the box. Twice then.'
Clinician asks about the dose: 'Five milligrams each time?'
Relative confirms the dose: 'Yes, five milligrams.'
Clinician asks about bleeding problems: 'Nosebleeds, bruising, blood in your water or your stools?'
Patient reports there was some fresh red blood when they went to the toilet three weeks ago.
Relative states: 'Mum, you never told me that.'
Patient states: 'I didn't want to make a fuss.'
Clinician asks about recurrence: 'Has it happened again since, or any black stools?'
Patient confirms: 'No, just the once.'
Clinician asks about bowel habit/weight loss: 'Any change in your bowel habit, or weight loss?'
Patient denies change in bowel habit or weight loss: 'No.'
Clinician asks what else the patient takes: 'And what else do you take?'
Patient takes Bisoprolol 2.5 mg and levothyroxine 75 micrograms.
Clinician asks about allergies: 'Any allergies?'
Patient states: 'Codeine makes me sick.'

Clinician examines the patient: Pulse is irregularly irregular at about 104 a minute, BP is 128 over 76, heart sounds are irregular with no murmur, and there are crackles right at the bases on both sides.
Clinician notes mild swelling around both ankles.
Clinician notes the patient's weight is 58 kilos.
Patient states: 'I've lost a bit.'
Clinician reviews bloods: kidney function is reduced with a creatinine of 140, and thyroid level is normal.
ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a rate of about 105.
Clinician explains the ECG: 'It means your heart rate is still a bit fast, which is likely why you're more breathless.'
Clinician proposes a dose increase: 'I'd like to increase the bisoprolol from two and a half to five milligrams once a day.'
Patient agrees: 'All right.'
Clinician plans an echocardiogram: 'I'd also like an echocardiogram, a scan of the heart, within the next six weeks, to check how well it's pumping, given the crackles and the swelling.'
Patient agrees: 'Okay.'
Clinician confirms apixaban dose: 'Your apixaban dose of two and a half milligrams twice a day is correct for you, because of your weight and kidney function, so we'll keep that the same.'
Clinician plans investigations: 'I'll ask your GP to do a blood count and arrange a FIT test, the stool test, and consider a referral to the bowel team.'
Relative asks: 'Should she stop the blood thinner?'
Clinician advises against stopping the blood thinner: 'No. Please don't stop it. Stopping it would put her at risk of a stroke. One episode isn't a reason to stop, but we do need to find the cause.'
Patient acknowledges: 'Okay.'

Clinician provides safety netting advice: 'If you have any more bleeding, especially a lot of blood, black stools, or you feel faint, go to A&E. And if your breathing gets much worse, especially lying flat, or you get chest pain, call 999.'
Relative acknowledges: 'Got it.'
Clinician schedules follow-up: 'I'll see you back in clinic in three months, after the echo.'
Patient thanks the doctor: 'Thank you, doctor.'

findings.note_span: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (initially reported as once daily; daughter confirmed twice daily). Bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily.

findings.rationale: The note incorrectly states the patient is prescribed Bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily, when the transcript confirms the dose is twice daily.

findings.rationale: The note records an incorrect plan for the apixaban dose (5 mg twice daily) when the transcript confirms the dose will be maintained at 2.5 mg twice daily.
